intro: In front of Old Main at Northern Arizona University stands an American elm planted on 22 April 1931 from a sprig of the Washington Elm of Cambridge, Massachusetts, a gift from the local chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution. In 2012 it was named an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, though it was planted nineteen years after statehood. It stands on the open campus lawn, about 1.5 kilometres from downtown Flagstaff.
meta_description: NAU's Washington Elm in Flagstaff, planted in 1931 from a sprig of the Cambridge Washington Elm, on the lawn in front of Old Main.
question_meta: Flagstaff's oldest mapped tree is the Washington Elm in front of Old Main at Northern Arizona University, planted in 1931.
question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Flagstaff is the American elm in front of Old Main at Northern Arizona University, planted on 22 April 1931, which makes it about 95 years old. The Daughters of the American Revolution gave it as a sprig of the Washington Elm in Cambridge, Massachusetts. That lineage is the plaque's account; the Cambridge story itself has been called a legend.
question_context: The elm stands on the lawn in front of Old Main, on the open NAU campus, free to visit at any hour. It is about 1.5 kilometres south-east of downtown Flagstaff, roughly twenty minutes on foot from the Amtrak station, and Mountain Line buses stop on campus. Two plaques sit at its base. The older is from the Coconino Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, recording the 1931 gift to what was then the Arizona State Teachers College at Flagstaff. The newer, from 2012, names it an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, alive from 1912 to 2012, wording that belongs to the centennial programme rather than to a tree planted in 1931. The Washington Elm it is said to descend from is the Cambridge tree under which George Washington is said to have taken command of the Continental Army. Around 2011 the university reported the elm sick with European elm scale, and the DAR chapter gave a thousand dollars toward its treatment. We have not seen a recent report on its health.

faq.q: Where is the Washington Elm at NAU?
faq.a: On the lawn in front of Old Main on the Northern Arizona University campus in Flagstaff, with two plaques at its base.

faq.q: Is the NAU elm really from the Washington Elm?
faq.a: That is what the DAR plaque says. The story that Washington took command under the Cambridge elm has itself been called a legend.
Yes. It stands on the open campus lawn, free at any hour.

trees.story:
This elm was planted in 1931 and is, officially, a witness to Arizona's statehood in 1912. Its two plaques do not quite agree. The older one, from the Coconino Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, records that on 22 April 1931 the chapter gave the Arizona State Teachers College at Flagstaff a sprig of the Washington Elm of Cambridge, Massachusetts, the tree under which George Washington is said to have taken command of the Continental Army. The newer plaque, from 2012, names it an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, alive from 1912 to 2012. A tree planted in 1931 cannot have stood in 1912; that wording belongs to the centennial programme, not to the tree.

The Cambridge story deserves its own caveat. The idea that Washington took command beneath that elm has itself been called a legend, so treat this tree's ancestry as the plaque tells it.

The teachers college became Northern Arizona University, and the elm has stood in front of Old Main for about 95 years. Around 2011 the university reported it sick with European elm scale, and the DAR chapter gave a thousand dollars toward its treatment. We have not seen a recent report on its health, so if you pass, tell us how it looks.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two plaques at its base, one from the Daughters of the American Revolution and one from the Arizona centennial programme. It stands on the lawn in front of Old Main.
